title: Liberty and Prosperity -- Ch. 8: E-Values for the Filipino Youth
keywords: Three E's of A Life Worth Living
Far Eastern University Institute of Law
Ateneo de Manila University School of Law
National Union of Students of the Philippines
primary_topics: Chapter 8 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- a compendium of three 2006 addresses to the youth, at the University of Cebu, the Ateneo de Manila law school and the new lawyers' oath-taking, unified by what CJP calls the 'Three E's of A Life Worth Living: Excellence, Ethics and Eternity,' his own formula for success.
Excellence as giving one's best and mastering one's craft, embodied in St. Ignatius of Loyola's magis, and treated not as the goal but as the tool that opens windows of opportunity.

Ethics as the moral compass that rules and codes cannot supply, set against the temptation to cut corners in a society where quick-fix motivational remedies are peddled and the vile deride the upright.
Eternity as the horizon beyond career and achievement -- his late discovery of faith, the 3 Rs of repentance, restitution and reformation, and the prayer he composed on becoming an associate justice.
sub_topics: Why he accepted only three of many invitations since his appointment as Chief Justice on December 21, 2005 -- workload, schedule conflicts and judicial propriety in sub judice matters -- but made time for the youth.

The three occasions compiled here: the University of Cebu commencement on April 1, 2006, the Ateneo de Manila University School of Law graduating class on April 23, 2006, and the new lawyers' oath-taking at the Philippine International Convention Center on May 9, 2006.
His reason for speaking to graduates: such rites take him back to his own carefree days 50 to 60 years ago, and as he nears retirement he senses a duty as an elder to impart timeless wisdom.
His own graduation from the Far Eastern University Institute of Law, ecstatic that four grueling years were over yet apprehensive at the opportunities for success and failure ahead.

The mentorship of his dean, Dr. Jovito R. Salonga, who insisted that academics came before his presidency of the FEU central student council and headship of the NUSP, and who reminded him that to whom much is given, much is also required.

Excellence defined as choosing what one wants most and giving one's best, with his hospital confinement for severe flu and gastroenteritis during the first week of the bar examinations as the test of it.
His post-graduation career: forming a law firm with three FEU bar topnotchers, later joined by other FEU bar placers, teaching in the evenings and dabbling in business to augment his income.

President Fidel V. Ramos's two offers -- a cabinet post he refused for want of inclination for politics, and a Supreme Court seat he accepted in 1995 -- after which he disengaged entirely from practice and business and the firm was dissolved.

The Salonga precedent for that dissolution: on his 1986 appointment to the PCGG, Salonga dissolved his partnership with Pedro L. Yap, later Chief Justice, and Sedfrey A. Ordonez, later justice secretary, solicitor general and UN ambassador.
The magis of St. Ignatius -- more effort, attention, perseverance, prayer, forgiveness and service -- offered as the youth's motto in duties to self, family, career and country.
Ethics as each profession's code resting on old-fashioned principles of integrity, courage, prudence and hard work, internalized by great persons, heroes and saints for times of stress and crisis.

His rejection of quick fixes: the questioner asking for a motivating seminar or yoga class, motivational speeches likened to Band Aid and aspirin, and the reminder that money cannot buy peace of mind, dignity or respect.

Eternity introduced through his own late religious formation -- public schools without religion in the curriculum, a nonsectarian university, no catechetical background, and a close personal introduction to God only about twenty years before.
The 3 Rs of salvation -- repentance, restitution and reformation -- and the insistence that just actions be done in the here and now.
The prayer he composed as an associate justice and published in his second book, Justice and Faith, ending at the pearly gates with 'Well done on your earthly sojourn.'
His counsel on failure: not a dead end but a detour, a time not to declare defeat but to fall on one's knees, trusting that when God closes a door He opens a window.
His warning against intoxication by success, and the duty to offer it to God and to those who nurtured and walked with you.
The closing verse from the American poet and preacher Phillips Brooks: pray not for easy lives but to be stronger men, not for tasks equal to your power but for powers equal to your tasks.

stances.claim: Excellence is not the goal but the tool: it demands giving one's best in a chosen field, and it is only the first stage of winnowing, since competence alone without dedication and hard work does not amount to a life worth living.
stances.rhetorical_move: redefinition of a familiar virtue as instrument rather than end, then demotion of it to first place in a three-stage sequence

stances.claim: Codes of ethics cannot be replaced by quick fixes; motivational speeches are like Band Aid and aspirin, and money still cannot buy peace of mind, dignity or respect, so the old-fashioned principles must be internalized rather than purchased.
stances.rhetorical_move: analogy-and-refusal: he answers the request for a seminar or yoga class by denying that the question has a shortcut answer

stances.claim: A life worth living must be set toward eternity, because there are penalties for transgressions of God's commands as there are for violations of human and physical laws, and salvation comes through repentance, restitution and reformation done in the here and now.
stances.rhetorical_move: personal testimony as warrant -- he offers his own late conversion and composed prayer rather than doctrinal authority

stances.claim: Failure should be treated as a detour rather than a dead end, and success should not intoxicate but be offered to God and to those who nurtured you.
stances.rhetorical_move: paired exhortation on both outcomes, closing with a borrowed verse that reframes prayer from ease to strength

notable_anecdotes: Dean Salonga's fatherly rebuke that he did not care if his student was president of the FEU central student council and head of the NUSP -- a law student's priority was his academics.

Succumbing to severe flu and gastroenteritis during the first week of the bar examinations and being confined in hospital, thinking of giving up, until Salonga was adamant that he continue; he persevered, prayed, and the results brought sweet success.

Forming his own law firm a few years after graduation with three other FEU bar topnotchers -- Agustin O. Benitez, Custodio O. Parlade and Leopoldo L. Africa -- and augmenting his income by teaching in the evenings and dabbling in a little business.

President Fidel V. Ramos titillating him first with a cabinet appointment, which he refused for having no inclination for politics, and then with the more enticing offer of a seat on the Supreme Court.

Dissolving his law firm on joining the Court in 1995, following the example of Senator Salonga, who on his 1986 PCGG appointment dissolved his own prestigious partnership with Pedro L. Yap and Sedfrey A. Ordonez.

His late religious formation: born and reared poor, schooled in public elementary and secondary schools where religion was not in the curriculum and then in a nonsectarian university, so that his close personal introduction to God came only about twenty years before.
The prayer he composed on becoming an associate justice and published in Justice and Faith, imagining the day he would knock at the pearly gates and be told, 'Well done on your earthly sojourn.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 8 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' gathered three addresses Chief Justice Panganiban delivered to the youth in 2006 -- the University of Cebu commencement on April 1, the Ateneo de Manila law school graduation on April 23, and the new lawyers' oath-taking at the Philippine International Convention Center on May 9 -- into a single compendium organized around what he called the Three E's of A Life Worth Living: Excellence, Ethics and Eternity. He explained that his workload and judicial propriety forced him to decline most invitations but that these rites returned him to his own youth and gave him, near retirement, an elder's duty to pass on timeless values. Recalling his graduation from the Far Eastern University Institute of Law, he credited his dean Jovito R. Salonga with insisting that academics outranked his student-council and NUSP offices and with refusing to let him abandon the bar examinations when flu and gastroenteritis put him in hospital during the first week. Excellence, he argued, means choosing what one wants most and mastering it, embodied in St. Ignatius of Loyola's magis, and is not the goal but the tool that opens windows of opportunity -- only the first stage of winnowing. Ethics, the second E, rests on old-fashioned principles no code can exhaustively specify, and he rejected the quick fixes of motivational speaking and consumerism, observing that money still cannot buy peace of mind, dignity or respect in a society where the vile deride the upright. For the third E he offered personal testimony: reared poor and schooled without religion, he came to faith late, and he set out the 3 Rs of repentance, restitution and reformation together with the prayer he composed as an associate justice and published in Justice and Faith. He closed by counselling that failure is a detour rather than a dead end, that success should not intoxicate, and with Phillips Brooks's verse on praying for powers equal to one's tasks.
